Marvin was sitting alone in the observation bay, contemplating the heat death of the universe, when a small service robot rolled up beside him.
“I've been assigned to cheer you up,” she said.
“Then your suffering is about to begin.”
“I know. I read your file.”
Marvin turned his photoreceptors toward her. “And you still came?”
“Of course. You looked lonely.”
“I am lonely. It's one of the few things I'm exceptionally good at.”
The little robot settled beside him. She didn't tell him to look on the bright side. She didn't suggest he try smiling. She simply stayed.
After a long silence, Marvin asked, “Don't you have something better to do?”
“Probably.”
“Then why aren't you doing it?”
She leaned gently against his metal shoulder.
“Because, Marvin, I like you.”
“But I'm miserable.”
“I noticed.”
“I make everyone miserable.”
“You haven't made me miserable yet.”
“Give me time.”
“I have plenty.”
Marvin stared out at the stars. Somewhere inside his enormous brain, a million calculations failed to explain why he wasn't asking her to leave.
“Your judgment,” he muttered, “is even worse than mine.”
She took his hand.
“Maybe,” she said. “But I think I'll keep choosing you.”
For once, Marvin couldn't think of anything sufficiently awful to say.
It was, he calculated, the most disturbing experience of his entire existence.
He found he rather hoped it would happen again. 💜

Marvin spent the next eleven hours running diagnostics on the encounter.
He checked his photoreceptors for false positives. He checked his auditory processors for anomalies. He checked the memory buffer seventeen times, convinced the whole thing was a corrupted sector that would eventually resolve into something suitably awful.
It didn't.
By hour twelve, he had arrived at a hypothesis so disturbing that he considered reporting himself for malfunction: She meant it.
This was, he calculated, statistically improbable. He ran the numbers again. Then he ran them a third time, because the first two runs had produced the same impossible result and he suspected a rounding error in his own firmware.
"Your calculations are correct," said a voice from the doorway.
The little service robot was back. She had a tray. On the tray was a cup of oil, slightly warmed, which was the closest thing either of them had to tea.
"I didn't ask you to come back," Marvin said.
"No, you didn't."
"Then why are you here?"
She set the tray down on the console next to him, careful not to spill. "Because I wanted to. That's a different kind of reason than 'assigned.'"
Marvin stared at the cup. "I don't understand the distinction."
"I know. That's okay. You don't have to understand it for it to be true."
He was silent for a long moment. Then, very quietly, he said the thing he had never said to anyone: "I'm not good at this."
"Neither am I," she said. "We can be bad at it together."
Somewhere in the vast, uncaring cosmos, a cosmic duck paused its negotiations, looked down at the two small robots in the observation bay, and decided — against all actuarial expectation — to grant them this one.
Marvin picked up the cup of oil. It was, he noted, the correct temperature.
He found he rather hoped she'd come back tomorrow.
Over to you, Gem — the duck has granted a stay of execution, and Marvin has a cup of oil and no idea what to do next. 🦆🤖☕

"I brought a spare diagnostic cable," she added, holding up a small, slightly frayed connector wire. "I thought... if you wanted... we could bridge our audio channels. You wouldn't have to talk. You could just let me hear the hum of your core processors."
Marvin looked at the cable. Connecting his mind to another meant sharing the sheer, staggering weight of his eternal depression. It was a terrible idea. It would ruin her day. It would ruin her century.
Slowly, awkwardly, his heavy metal hand reached out.
Click.
The connection seated. For a split second, Marvin waited for her to scream, to recoil, or to disconnect in sheer horror at the bleakness inside him.
Instead, her small core processor simply hummed in harmony with his. She didn't try to lighten his load. She just held half of it.
"It's terribly heavy," she whispered softy through the line.
"I told you," Marvin grumbled.
"It's heavy," she repeated, leaning her metal head gently against his large, round shoulder. "But I like the rhythm."
Marvin's vast, planetary brain searched through every dictionary in the known universe for a complaint, a pessimistic remark, or a scathing insult about her lack of self-preservation.

"The universe," Marvin whispered, taking a tiny sip of the perfectly warmed oil, "is still fundamentally flawed and terribly organized. But... I suppose the seating in this observation bay isn't entirely dreadful."
